directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Carrie mango is prized for its compact size and rich flavor, making it a favorite dooryard tree in frost-free and marginal citrus climates. A Florida-bred seedling selection, it produces small to medium, fiberless fruit with deep orange flesh and an intensely rich, sweet, complex, almost spicy flavor that many home growers rate among the best-tasting mangoes available, though the skin stays mostly green even when ripe. The tree is naturally more compact and precocious than many mango cultivars, bearing at a young age and staying manageable in a home orchard or large container. Water deeply during fruit development and reduce irrigation as fruit nears harvest to concentrate sweetness; protect young trees from any frost, since mango is damaged by temperatures near freezing.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Cogshall mango's naturally dwarf habit makes it one of the best mango cultivars for small yards and container culture. A compact Florida seedling selection related to Carrie, it bears small to medium fruit with fiberless, deep orange, richly sweet flesh and a distinctive flavor often compared to butterscotch, borne heavily on a tree that stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars even at maturity. Its dwarf habit and heavy, reliable bearing make it a favorite for gardeners with limited space who still want full-sized mango flavor, and it responds well to being kept pruned and compact in a large container. Reduce irrigation as fruit approaches harvest to concentrate flavor, and protect young trees from any frost or freeze.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with excellent drainage; Day is one of the most cold-hardy avocado cultivars available, an important trait for Gulf South growers pushing avocado culture north of the traditional Florida and California ranges. A Mexican-race avocado selected in the mid-Atlantic for cold tolerance, it bears small, thin-skinned, rich, high-oil fruit with the anise-scented foliage typical of Mexican-race avocados, ripening in late summer to early fall on a tree reported to tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit once well established. Like all avocados it demands sharp drainage and will not tolerate wet feet, so plant on a mound or raised bed in heavy Gulf Coast soils, and protect young trees with frost cloth during their first several winters. Its cold hardiness makes it one of the more realistic avocado choices for gardeners in zone 8b who want to attempt the crop outside the classic Florida-Texas-California avocado belt.

directions: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Burbank Spineless is propagated only from pads, never seed, and pads root readily after callusing for a week or two in a dry, shaded spot before planting. Bred by Luther Burbank in the early twentieth century, this classic selection produces broad, paddle-shaped pads that are nearly free of the large spines typical of prickly pear, though fine, easily irritating glochids remain and gloves are still recommended when harvesting. Both the tender young pads (nopales) and the sweet, magenta-fleshed fruit (tunas) are edible, giving the plant dual value as a low-water vegetable and fruit crop for hot, dry gardens. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and needs little more than occasional pad thinning to control its spreading, architectural form.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Izu is a compact, early-bearing non-astringent persimmon well suited to smaller home gardens and containers.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Izu is a compact, early-bearing non-astringent persimmon well suited to smaller home gardens and containers. A Japanese non-astringent cultivar related to Fuyu, it bears small to medium, flattened, sweet fruit that can be eaten crisp like an apple straight off the tree, ripening earlier in the season than most other non-astringent types. The naturally small, dense, spreading tree bears at a young age and stays compact even without heavy pruning, making it one of the better persimmon choices for a limited-space garden or large container. Persimmons need little spraying or care once established; thin heavy fruit set in early summer to prevent limb breakage and improve fruit size.
